Output: "To answer this question, we need to examine the nature of both the Slaughter-House Cases and United States v. Darby Lumber Co. to determine if they both involved civil rights law.\n\nThe Slaughter-House Cases (83 U.S. 36, 1873) were a pivotal case in early civil rights law. They involved a challenge to a Louisiana law that granted a monopoly on the slaughterhouse business in New Orleans, which led to a discussion on the interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. This amendment is crucial in civil rights law as it addresses citizenship, equal protection under the law, and the protection of civil rights. The case is significant in the context of civil rights because it was one of the first to interpret the scope of the Fourteenth Amendment, particularly its impact on the rights of states versus the federal government.\n\nUnited States v. Darby Lumber Co. (312 U.S. 100, 1941), on the other hand, involved the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. This case was about the power of Congress under the Commerce Clause to regulate employment conditions, including minimum wages and maximum hours. While it is fundamentally a labor law case, it has implications for civil rights in the broader sense, as fair labor standards can be seen as a component of economic rights, which are closely related to civil rights. The case upheld the constitutionality of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which was a significant victory for workers' rights and, by extension, civil rights.\n\nConsidering these explanations, both cases have connections to civil rights law, although the Slaughter-House Cases are more directly related to the interpretation of constitutional amendments that explicitly address civil rights, whereas United States v. Darby Lumber Co. deals with labor rights, which are a subset of economic rights closely tied to the broader concept of civil rights.\n\nAnswer: Yes"
